headline: Massachusetts declares energy emergency, rolls out winter bill relief
dek: Gov. Maura Healey says the package will deliver nearly $150 million in savings through new heating-oil aid, larger HEAP benefits and temporary electric-bill charge relief.
body: Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey declared a state of energy emergency Monday and announced a package aimed at reducing winter heating and electric costs for households and businesses. The administration says the measures will deliver nearly $150 million in relief, including new help for some middle-income households that previously fell outside the state's main heating-assistance program. The announcement is from the [Massachusetts governor's office](https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-announces-new-winter-energy-bill-relief-for-massachusetts-families).

The most visible change is a new home-heating-oil benefit for approximately 50,000 households. Healey's office says the benefit is intended for middle-class oil-heated homes that did not qualify for existing assistance. [Boston 25 News](https://www.boston25news.com/news/local/gov-healey-declares-state-emergency-over-winter-energy-costs-massachusetts/QXTBNNQIEVBCTACFFICWIELRCM/) reported that the new program is aimed at households between 60% and 100% of state median income and could provide a one-time benefit of up to $680. The station said the benefit is expected to be available in December and run through April 30, 2027. That makes the program broader than traditional low-income assistance, but it does not mean every oil-heated household will automatically receive a payment; eligibility and application rules still govern access.

The plan also adds $15 million to the Home Energy Assistance Program, or HEAP, for about 156,000 low-income households. Boston 25 reported that the resulting support is expected to range from roughly $525 to $1,200 per household, with a 20% increase for homes using oil and a 15% increase for homes heated by utilities. The administration says homeowners and renters can apply, including households whose heat is included in rent, and that applicants do not need to be receiving public assistance or already have an unpaid heating bill. The heating-assistance period runs from Nov. 1, 2026, through April 30, 2027, according to the state's program information.

The relief is not limited to heating fuel. The state plans to use $80 million to cover the Solar Massachusetts Renewable Target charge on residential and commercial electric bills for three months, from January through March 2027. The SMART program supports qualifying solar projects, but its costs normally appear as a charge on customer bills. Covering the charge with state money would temporarily shift that cost away from ratepayers; it is not a permanent change to the solar-incentive program. Healey also said the administration will cut the Alternative Portfolio Standard by 50% this winter, a regulatory move the state estimates would provide another $20 million in ratepayer relief.

The emergency declaration activates Massachusetts protections against price gouging for petroleum products. Healey directed state agencies to monitor, investigate and enforce rules against excessive or misleading fuel prices. That authority matters as households prepare for deliveries, but the declaration does not set a single statewide retail price for heating oil or guarantee that every supplier will charge the same amount. A family's final bill will still depend on its fuel use, supplier, delivery terms and the price when it orders.

The administration is pairing the state measures with a private fundraising effort. Healey, Congressman Joe Kennedy and Citizens Energy Corporation announced an Emergency Winter Warmth Fund, with Citizens Energy planning to contribute $100,000. The fund is meant to support existing assistance programs for low-income households as well as the new middle-income heating-oil benefit. It is additional charitable support, not a replacement for HEAP or for the federal funding that underwrites the state's main assistance program.

Residents do not have to wait for every new piece of the package before seeking help that already exists. The state's [Home Energy Assistance Program information](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/learn-about-home-energy-assistance-heap) explains that HEAP is free for eligible households, can help with oil, electricity, natural gas, propane and other primary heating sources, and is administered through local agencies. Those agencies can explain current income rules, application steps and emergency options. The program page is the right starting point for a household seeking assistance, but it is not a guarantee that a resident qualifies for the new middle-income oil benefit or for the same level of help as a HEAP participant.

Healey also asked Congress for $3 billion in additional emergency funding for the federal Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, which would raise the national program's funding to $7 billion. That request is not approved money, so the state's immediate plan and the federal appeal are separate tracks. The practical timeline is clearer: the existing and expanded heating assistance covers November through April, the new oil benefit is expected to start in December, and electric-charge relief is planned for the first three months of 2027. Massachusetts households should check the official program details as agencies publish the application process, because the announcement establishes the policy direction but does not make every household eligible for every form of relief.
author: NorthEast News Desk
